content: Hirsutism is a common and often distressing endocrine condition in women that can be challenging to manage. Cyproterone acetate, an anti-androgen, is frequently prescribed for the treatment of hirsutism, typically in combination with ethinyl estradiol. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of cyproterone acetate, either as a standalone treatment or in combination with ethinyl estradiol, in reducing excessive hair growth in women with hirsutism caused by ovarian hyperandrogenism. The Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group trials register was searched up to June 4, 2002. This register includes data from systematic searches of databases such as MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PsycINFO, and CENTRAL, as well as handsearching of journals, conference proceedings, and grey literature. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing cyproterone acetate (with or without ethinyl estradiol) to placebo or other drug therapies for hirsutism were identified. The inclusion criteria for the review were RCTs that compared: 1. Cyproterone acetate to placebo. 2. Cyproterone acetate combined with ethinyl estradiol to placebo. 3. Cyproterone acetate combined with ethinyl estradiol to cyproterone acetate alone. 4. Cyproterone acetate (with or without ethinyl estradiol) to other medical therapies for hirsutism. A total of 11 studies met the inclusion criteria, of which 9 were included in the review. Two studies were excluded due to insufficient information. Only one study included more than 100 participants. The primary outcomes assessed were subjective improvement in hirsutism, changes in Ferriman-Gallwey scores, alterations in linear hair growth and hair shaft diameter, changes in endocrine parameters, treatment-related side effects, and withdrawal rates during therapy. The review found no clinical trials that compared cyproterone acetate alone to placebo. One small study compared cyproterone acetate combined with ethinyl estradiol to placebo, showing a significant subjective reduction in hair growth with cyproterone acetate therapy, although the confidence intervals were wide. No studies directly compared cyproterone acetate alone to cyproterone acetate combined with ethinyl estradiol for the treatment of hirsutism. When cyproterone acetate was compared to other drug therapies, such as ketoconazole, spironolactone, flutamide, finasteride, and GnRH analogues, no significant differences in clinical outcomes were observed. However, there were endocrinological differences in androgen and estrogen levels between the various drug therapies. The data were insufficient to evaluate differences in side effects between cyproterone acetate and other treatments. The authors concluded that cyproterone acetate combined with ethinyl estradiol leads to a subjective improvement in hirsutism compared to placebo. However, no clinical differences in outcomes were demonstrated between cyproterone acetate and other medical therapies. This lack of observed differences may be attributed to the small sample sizes of the studies, the absence of standardized assessment methods, and the lack of objective measures of improvement in hirsutism. The endocrinological effects of the various drug therapies reflect their mechanisms of action. Larger, well-designed studies are necessary to compare the efficacy and safety profiles of different treatments for hirsutism.
